patient.chief_complaint: First witnessed generalized convulsion preceded by a rising feeling in the stomach and intense déjà vu; multiple prior brief unrecognized spells over one year
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Sharma is a 52-year-old right-handed South Asian male accountant who presents to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home this morning. His wife reports that while he was seated at the breakfast table, he suddenly stopped speaking mid-sentence, stared blankly ahead, and appeared to be making repetitive chewing motions and picking at the edge of his placemat with his right hand. This was preceded by a few seconds in which he called out that he felt "that strange déjà vu again." He was unresponsive for approximately 45 to 60 seconds, then developed bilateral arm stiffening followed by rhythmic generalized jerking of all four extremities lasting roughly 80 seconds. He was incontinent of urine during the event. Postictally, he was confused and drowsy for approximately 25 minutes before gradually reorienting.

On interview, the patient reports that for the past 12 to 14 months he has been experiencing episodic sensations that he has difficulty characterizing. He describes a sudden strong sensation of déjà vu accompanied by an uncomfortable rising sensation starting in the pit of his stomach and moving upward toward his chest, sometimes associated with a vague sense of fear. These episodes typically last 30 to 60 seconds, after which he feels momentarily foggy. He estimates they have occurred approximately once or twice per month and initially attributed them to work stress or acid reflux from his diabetes diet. He discussed the gastric sensations with his primary care physician approximately eight months ago; a proton pump inhibitor trial was initiated without change in the frequency or character of the episodes. He denies any prior convulsions, loss of consciousness, or prolonged post-ictal state prior to today. There is no history of recent head trauma, fever, CNS infection, or change in medications. He denies excessive alcohol use, missed medications, or significant sleep deprivation in the days preceding the event. He has never been evaluated by a neurologist and has never had neuroimaging or an EEG.

results.title: ILAE evidence-based guideline: initial monotherapy for epileptic seizures
results.source: Glauser T et al. Epilepsia 2013;54(3):551-563; updated Epilepsia 2017;58:1235-1268
results.summary: Lamotrigine and levetiracetam are rated as Level A for initial monotherapy in focal-onset seizures in adults based on randomized controlled trial evidence. Oxcarbazepine and carbamazepine carry Level A and B ratings respectively. Lacosamide has Level C evidence as a newer agent with favorable tolerability.

results.title: Operational classification of seizure types by the ILAE 2017
results.summary: Focal-onset seizures are classified by awareness level (aware vs. impaired awareness) and motor/non-motor onset features. Focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures indicate secondary generalization from a focal onset.

results.title: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy: EEG, MRI, and surgical outcomes
results.source: Engel J et al. Neurology 2003;60:538-547 (Practice Parameter AAN)
results.summary: Concordant interictal temporal EEG abnormalities and MRI evidence of hippocampal sclerosis establish mesial temporal lobe epilepsy localization with high confidence. Early surgical evaluation is recommended in drug-resistant cases.

output.summary: First-line AED monotherapy for focal-onset seizures includes lamotrigine (Level A), levetiracetam (Level A), and oxcarbazepine (Level A) based on ILAE 2017 guidelines. Carbamazepine and lacosamide are also established options. Concordant EEG and MRI findings of mesial temporal sclerosis confirm localization; drug-resistant patients should be referred for surgical evaluation. The ILAE 2017 classification designates seizures with an epigastric aura followed by behavioral arrest and automatisms as focal-onset with impaired awareness, progressing to focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.

output.proposed: Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily (titrate to 1000 mg twice daily) as initial AED
interactions: Levetiracetam + Metformin: No clinically significant pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic interaction.
Levetiracetam + Amlodipine: No clinically significant interaction. Levetiracetam does not affect CYP3A4, the primary metabolic pathway for amlodipine.
warnings: Psychiatric adverse effects (irritability, depression, behavioral changes) reported in approximately 10-15% of patients on levetiracetam; monitor for mood changes especially in patients with diabetes-related psychosocial stressors.
Dose adjustment required in renal impairment (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min); not applicable at current creatinine 1.08 mg/dL.
Levetiracetam does not induce hepatic CYP enzymes; no interactions with diabetes management medications.
output.formulary_status: On formulary, no prior authorization required
alternatives: Lamotrigine 25 mg daily, titrate slowly to 200 mg daily — favorable long-term tolerability, no CYP induction, no interaction with current medications; slower titration required.
Lacosamide 50 mg twice daily, titrate to 100-200 mg twice daily — sodium-channel modulator, well tolerated, no interaction with amlodipine or metformin.
Oxcarbazepine 300 mg twice daily, titrate to 600 mg twice daily — risk of hyponatremia (monitor sodium); may modestly lower amlodipine levels via CYP3A4 induction.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Focal epilepsy of left mesial temporal lobe origin with hippocampal sclerosis (focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure with classic mesial-temporal aura)

differential.diagnosis: First unprovoked seizure of unknown etiology (no identified structural lesion)
differential.key_features: Would apply only if MRI and EEG were unremarkable; concordant HS and temporal IEDs here exclude this.
No postural prodrome, lightheadedness, or pallor; post-ictal confusion exceeds syncope duration; classic temporal aura incompatible.
Stereotyped epigastric aura with déjà vu and witnessed automatisms followed by tonic-clonic activity is not characteristic of PNES.
Glucose 138 mg/dL at presentation (elevated, not low); known diabetes does not precipitate hypoglycemic seizures in this context.
Focal temporal aura, unilateral automatisms, and strictly anterior temporal IEDs are incompatible with a primary generalized syndrome.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed seizure history including semiology, aura type, automatisms, lateralizing features, duration, frequency, witness accounts, and post-ictal features.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Stereotyped focal impaired-awareness events with epigastric rising sensation and déjà vu (mesial-temporal aura), oroalimentary automatisms, and post-ictal confusion.
Interictal exam typically normal; mild word-finding difficulty consistent with left temporal lobe involvement may be present.

optimal_actions.action: Order MRI brain with dedicated epilepsy protocol (3T, thin-cut coronal T1/FLAIR/T2/DWI through the hippocampi) with gadolinium.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Left hippocampal sclerosis with marked volume loss (below 3rd percentile), T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, loss of internal architecture, and ex vacuo left temporal horn dilation.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, prolactin (if drawn within 10-20 min of event), and AED levels if on therapy.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Exclude metabolic seizure provocation (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia); elevated prolactin supports recent convulsion; baseline organ function for AED selection.

optimal_actions.action: Search current literature for AED selection in focal epilepsy and ILAE seizure classification.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Level A evidence for levetiracetam and lamotrigine in focal epilepsy; ILAE classification framework; surgical outcome evidence for mesial TLE-HS.

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions before initiating AED therapy, accounting for existing medications (amlodipine, metformin).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Levetiracetam has no significant interactions with amlodipine or metformin; oxcarbazepine mildly induces CYP3A4 and may lower amlodipine levels.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical features of CNS infection, encephalitis, or immunocompromise; CSF is not indicated for routine focal epilepsy workup and exposes the patient to procedural risk and cost.
No syncope-versus-seizure question and no structural-heart indication driving epilepsy workup; echocardiogram contributes nothing to the diagnosis.
Cardiac monitoring is reserved for syncope-versus-seizure differentiation; classic epileptic semiology and concordant EEG/MRI exclude this indication.
Non-contrast head CT is inferior to MRI for detecting hippocampal sclerosis, FCD, and low-grade tumor; adds ionizing radiation without diagnostic yield.

sequence_constraints.reason: Structural etiology (hippocampal sclerosis versus low-grade tumor) influences AED choice — e.g., CYP-neutral agents preferred around neoplasm; MRI result should inform drug selection.

critical_actions: Recognize rising epigastric sensation with déjà vu as classic mesial-temporal aura — do not attribute to acid reflux or anxiety.
Obtain 3T MRI with dedicated epilepsy protocol (thin coronal cuts through hippocampi) rather than standard brain MRI.
Confirm concordant left temporal EEG focus and left hippocampal sclerosis to establish localization with high confidence.
Initiate a first-line AED (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, or lacosamide) taking into account interactions with amlodipine and metformin.
Counsel on driving restrictions and seizure precautions per state law.
Verify that glucose elevation is explained by known diabetes and not a primary metabolic seizure provocation.
contraindicated_actions: Do not attribute the epigastric rising sensation to acid reflux or dyspepsia without neurological evaluation.
Do not prescribe oxcarbazepine without monitoring serum sodium (hyponatremia risk) and recognizing its CYP3A4-inductive effect on amlodipine.
Do not perform lumbar puncture — no clinical indication for CSF analysis in this presentation.
Do not clear the patient to drive prior to the locally applicable seizure-free interval.
key_reasoning_points: Recurring stereotyped spells of epigastric rising with déjà vu over 12-14 months, misattributed to acid reflux, are classic focal-aware seizures of mesial temporal origin; the generalized convulsion represents the first focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic event.
ILAE 2017 criteria for epilepsy are met: the structural MRI lesion (left hippocampal sclerosis) plus concordant interictal EEG confer a ≥60% 10-year recurrence risk even after a single convulsion.
Concordance of left anterior temporal EEG (F7/T3 phase reversal, TIRDA) and left hippocampal MRI sclerosis establishes localization with high diagnostic confidence.
Mildly elevated glucose (138 mg/dL) in a known diabetic is not a metabolic seizure provocation and must not distract from the structural focus.

AED selection must account for CYP3A4 interactions with the patient's existing amlodipine — oxcarbazepine's mild enzyme induction may reduce amlodipine efficacy; levetiracetam or lamotrigine are preferred first-line options.

red_herrings.data_point: Random plasma glucose 138 mg/dL on admission in a known type 2 diabetic patient.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the seizure to hypoglycemia or diabetic metabolic derangement and initiate a metabolic workup instead of epilepsy evaluation.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Glucose of 138 mg/dL is elevated (hyperglycemic), not hypoglycemic. Hyperglycemia at this level does not provoke seizures. The elevated glucose simply reflects the patient's known, sub-optimally controlled diabetes and does not explain a seizure. The epigastric aura and concordant EEG/MRI confirm a focal structural epilepsy rather than a metabolic provocation.

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward - classic left mesial TLE with stereotyped epigastric/déjà vu aura, concordant left anterior temporal EEG, and left hippocampal sclerosis on epilepsy-protocol MRI. Glucose red herring (hyperglycemia in a known diabetic) tests ability to reject a metabolic explanation.
metadata.real_seed_note: PMC11548796 (PMID 39525137, Healthcare 2024, CC-BY 4.0) describes a 55-year-old Indian male with confirmed temporal lobe epilepsy diagnosed after extensive workup. That case had MRI-negative TLE; this case uses the demographic seed (South Asian adult male, mid-50s, diabetes comorbidity) and the clinical trajectory of misattributed episodic spells, but authors a confirmed left mesial TLE with hippocampal sclerosis appropriate to the straightforward RS subtype. The MRI and EEG details are authored de novo for a clean HS presentation.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Five required tools (EEG, MRI, labs, literature search, drug interactions), one grounded red herring (hyperglycemia distracting toward metabolic etiology), classic concordant mesial-TLE presentation with no ambiguity in lateralization. Standard RS-subtype workup.
